items.gist: The passage opens by announcing the kalādhvā and situates kalā as a tattva distinguished within its own varga, set apart from other vargas.

items.topic: Views on kalā: śakti or convention
items.gist: It presents differing views—kalā as subtle śakti or as a convention established by Śiva for initiation—while arguing the underlying object is not different.
It lists the fourfold progression to Śiva beyond kalā and emphasizes Śiva’s unrestricted freedom and self-manifestation.
It discusses the aṇḍa as world-division cause and covering, noting that even in the Śiva tattva there is no real obstruction.
The teachers’ view presents the five elements as directly perceived, with thirty tattvas arising from differentiation and Śiva-anta pañcaka.
It states that five tattvas pervade the world and then distinguishes Śiva tattva, paraśiva as thirty-seventh, and the unbounded thirty-eighth.
It explains the thirty-sixth tattva and the further thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth levels, where knowing and being-known are refined.
It traces subtle sensory elements to sparśa and saṃvitti, then connects vindu, nāda, rūpa, and rasa to the trika tattva scheme.
It presents vijñānākala through Śiva as three tattvas and explains how tattvādhva extends from thirty-six to one tattva according to the disciple’s capacity.
It describes Śiva resting in himself and the three adhvas by coarseness and subtlety, then begins the mātṛ portion in three forms.
It identifies pada with mantra and explains how varṇādhva arises in the mātṛ portion, culminating in sixteen letters.
It summarizes the correspondences among varṇa, mantra, and pada, attributing the concise teaching to Abhinavagupta for students.
It presents the whole adhva as Bhairava’s non-dual activity and traces the movement from mātṛ form to mantra and pada.

items.topic: Mātṛ rest and pada as pramāṇa
items.gist: It explains the mātṛ’ s rest through varṇas and concludes that pada is the form of pramāṇa, retaining pramāṇa-nature in meyatā.
